title: Hippocratic Growth
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: A teacher-authored piece argues that growth mindset, whatever its definitional merit, has become a sloganistic classroom crutch that excuses weak instruction rather than improving it. The author accepts Carol Dweck's core claim as technically true but argues the popularized "power of yet" message misleads students into thinking time alone, rather than deliberate effort and structure, will close the gap. Citing the EEF's 2019 finding that growth-mindset training changed student beliefs about intelligence but produced no measurable learning gains, the piece argues the concept lets teachers blame students' "not yet" rather than their own instructional or curricular gaps. A sustained running analogy—comparing training for a faster 5K to spaced retrieval and structured intervention in the classroom—makes the case that improvement requires deliberate practice, not just belief in future improvement. The essay closes with a medical analogy: framing uncritical growth-mindset messaging as a violation of a Hippocratic "do no harm" standard in teaching. It fits Education - Learning & Curriculum for its direct engagement with cognitive-science research and classroom pedagogy around a specific instructional framework.
points: Argues that growth mindset, while definitionally reasonable, functions in practice as a sloganistic excuse that lets teachers offload responsibility for student non-mastery onto "not yet."
Cites the EEF's 2019 finding that growth-mindset training changed students' beliefs about intelligence but had no measurable impact on learning outcomes.
Uses a personal running analogy (a 17:07 5K personal best versus current fitness) to argue that improvement requires structured, deliberate practice, not just belief that improvement is possible.
Contrasts growth mindset's "wait for yet" framing with the fixed realities of school schedules, grades, and assessment deadlines.
Frames the critique as a medical "do no harm" argument: telling students to "just have a growth mindset" without concrete instructional intervention can actively harm them.
quotes: Growth mindset despite sounding promising in reality often leads to a sloganistic approach to student ability and effort which can create complacency and stagnation.
The real problem with a growth mindset is that it gives teachers a get out of jail free card for students lack of success and learning.
Furthermore, Carol Dweck's original study's results have been unable to be replicated in any future study.
